surface_mechanism_description: The surface reaction mechanism involves the interaction of the precursor with surface hydroxyl groups, followed by a rehydroxylation step. For compound 1, ozone (O3) reacts with the surface, leading to the formation of MoO2.48N0.18 and the desorption of protonated ligands. For compound 2, water (H2O) reacts with the surface, leading to the formation of WO3 and the desorption of protonated ligands. The mechanism for compound 1 involves ligand decomposition and rehydroxylation via H-atom abstraction from the decomposed ligand, while for compound 2, rehydroxylation occurs directly through reaction with H2O.
evidence: The surface reaction mechanism is described in the text as follows: 'Mass loss during the “B” reaction (Δm2) averages 9.5 ± 0.5 ng/cm2, corresponding to a loss of 54% of the parent compound mass per reaction. The average total mass gain per cycle (Δm3 = Δm1 – Δm2) is 8.1 ± 1.0 ng/cm2, yielding a theoretical surface coverage rate of ca. 0.3 Mo/nm2 per cycle. This number is approximate, however, as an unknown mass of decomposed ligand is also incorporated in the film. As compound 1 contains ca. 75% ligand mass (assuming oxomoieties are retained after deposition), the calculated mass loss of 54% is consistent with ligand decomposition on the substrate surface during ALD. This is confirmed by XPS, which indicates the presence of C and N contamination, as well as the presence of N incorporated in the film after annealing (SI, Figure S6-S7). The group of Gordon has reported similar findings for films grown with O3 at temperatures below 320 ˚C. 82 From these data, it is reasonable to speculate that the mechanism of surface rehydroxylation must occur as a result of H-atom abstraction from the decomposed ligand on the surface of the film, leading to a proposed surface structure as shown in Scheme 3. 83 The mechanism in Scheme 3 is proposed on the basis of previous studies 82, 84, 85 that show O3 to react with ligands in a combustive manner, with rehydroxylation occurring as a result of the ligand decomposition. ... For compound 2, the reaction with H2O leads to the formation of WO3 and the desorption of protonated ligands. The mass loss during the “B” reaction (Δm2) averages 8.6 ± 0.8 ng/cm2, corresponding to an average loss of 65% of the parent compound mass per cycle. The average total mass gain per cycle (Δm3 = Δm1 – Δm2) is 4.7 ± 0.7 ng/cm2, yielding a theoretical surface coverage rate of ~ 0.1 W/nm2-cy. Compound 2 contains ca. 61% ligand mass, in good agreement with the mass loss observed via QCM. While the mass loss during reaction B indicates the ligand remains absorbed on the surface after deposition of W during reaction A, it does not appear to decompose in the same manner as it does when O3 is introduced into the system. Instead, rehydroxylation must occur instead via direct reaction of H2O with tungsten oxo groups, as shown in Scheme 4. Katrib et al. have explored the reactivity of supported tungsten-oxo groups and observed similar surface structures, 113-117 and it is well-known that during the aggregation of polyoxotungstates, tungsten-oxo groups convert to dihydroxy groups under aqueous conditions. 118-120'
